title: Selecting the teaching priority
stem: Before discharge, a client correctly demonstrates wound cleansing, dressing placement and moisture protection and has supplies. They cannot identify concerning changes. What teaching has highest priority?
options: Reconfirm where replacement dressings can be purchased
Review changes requiring help and the contact route
Repeat the demonstrated dressing sequence
Rehearse shower-cover placement once more
why: Supply access is already established and is not the demonstrated gap.
Recognition and access teaching addresses the remaining safety need.
The routine sequence has already been demonstrated correctly.
Moisture protection is established; escalation knowledge remains missing.
takeaway: Prioritize the demonstrated safety gap after routine skills are established.
learningObjective: Prioritize the demonstrated safety gap after routine skills are established.

title: Assessing practical learning barriers
stem: A client correctly describes medication timing, has supplies, opens packaging easily and reports no adverse effects. Morning doses are missed while helping a spouse dress. What should the nurse explore first?
options: Whether prescription costs are creating a barrier
Whether medication effects discourage morning use
How dosing fits the caregiving routine
Whether a different container would be easier to open
why: Current supply is available and cost is not the stated obstacle.
No adverse effects are reported; the timing conflict is explicit.
The missed doses coincide with competing caregiving tasks.
Packaging is manageable and does not explain this pattern.
takeaway: Target the practical barrier supported by the client's account.
learningObjective: Target the practical barrier supported by the client's account.

title: Independent monitoring with arthritis
stem: A client understands glucose monitoring but cannot open the current strip package because of arthritis. They want independence and have no helper at testing times. What is the best next plan?
options: Assess accessible packaging or a suitable alternative device
Ask a relative to prepare every test at dosing time
Repeat practice opening the same package for another week
Arrange all monitoring through scheduled home visits
why: An equipment adaptation directly addresses the barrier while preserving the stated goal.
No helper is available at the required times.
Repetition alone may not overcome the mechanical limitation.
Full service takeover may be unnecessary if a feasible adaptation exists.
takeaway: Assess equipment adaptations before replacing feasible independent self-care.
learningObjective: Assess equipment adaptations before replacing feasible independent self-care.

title: Evaluating a practical skill
stem: After catheter-care teaching, a client describes every step correctly but contaminates the equipment during practice. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: The teaching objective is met because recall is accurate
Another pamphlet is sufficient evidence of correction
Performance can be assumed to improve at home
Practical competence requires further coached practice and reassessment
why: Accurate recall does not establish safe task performance.
Receiving information is not evidence of corrected technique.
Unobserved future improvement cannot be assumed.
The observed error identifies a specific skill needing practice.
takeaway: Evaluate demonstrated performance separately from verbal knowledge.
learningObjective: Evaluate demonstrated performance separately from verbal knowledge.

title: Interpreter-supported teaching
stem: A client prefers a language the nurse does not speak. Which approaches support accurate teaching with a qualified interpreter? Select all that apply.
options: Speak directly to the client
Pause after short segments
Ask the interpreter to decide which care instructions matter
Use a family member to verify confidential answers without asking the client
why: Direct engagement preserves the therapeutic relationship.
Short segments support accurate interpretation and questions.
Clinical priorities remain the responsibility of the care team and client.
Involving relatives requires attention to client preference and privacy.
takeaway: Use qualified interpretation while communicating directly with the client.
learningObjective: Use qualified interpretation while communicating directly with the client.

title: A decimal misunderstanding in measurement
stem: A caregiver is supplied an appropriate oral syringe for a prescribed 0.5 mL dose but draws to 5 mL during practice. What should the nurse do first?
options: Have the caregiver read the dose and explain the chosen marking
Request a new medication concentration immediately
Replace the syringe with a measuring cup
Repeat the medicine's purpose before another demonstration
why: The tenfold discrepancy requires identifying and correcting the decimal or marking misunderstanding.
A concentration change may not resolve the demonstrated interpretation problem.
A cup is less suitable for a small volume and does not correct the misunderstanding.
The medicine's purpose does not explain the incorrect volume selection.
takeaway: Clarify the meaning of the prescribed volume when demonstration reveals a decimal error.
learningObjective: Clarify the meaning of the prescribed volume when demonstration reveals a decimal error.

title: Organizing complex instructions
stem: A client receiving instructions from three services says the separate leaflets conflict and they cannot identify the first home-care task. What is most useful?
options: Review all leaflets verbally in one uninterrupted session
Provide the complete technical discharge summary
Create a coordinated prioritized action checklist and practise its first steps
Give a separate booklet from each additional specialist
why: An uninterrupted review may preserve the fragmentation and overload.
A technical summary may not translate recommendations into usable actions.
Coordination resolves sequence and consistency before practice checks usability.
More disconnected information may worsen the stated problem.
takeaway: Coordinate competing instructions into a usable prioritized action plan.
learningObjective: Coordinate competing instructions into a usable prioritized action plan.

title: Teaching after a sensory change
stem: A client newly using reading glasses is learning ostomy care and avoids the printed guide. What should the nurse assess first?
options: Whether the client can see the material and equipment comfortably
Whether the client agrees with every instruction
Whether family help is available for reading the guide
What the client already knows about ostomy care
why: Visual access may explain avoidance and can often be improved.
Agreement does not establish access to the teaching materials.
Family support may help, but the new visual barrier should first be assessed directly.
Prior knowledge matters, but new glasses and avoided print specifically suggest an access issue.
takeaway: Assess sensory access before interpreting limited engagement as resistance.
learningObjective: Assess sensory access before interpreting limited engagement as resistance.

title: A missed learning goal
stem: A client agreed to practise a dressing change but cannot complete it after teaching. What is the best nursing response?
options: Record the goal as achieved because teaching occurred
Label the client unwilling before reassessment
Repeat the identical session without examining the difficulty
Identify the difficult steps and adapt the teaching plan
why: Teaching delivery is not equivalent to learning achievement.
Difficulty may reflect a skill, access or readiness problem.
Unchanged repetition may leave the actual barrier untouched.
Step-specific assessment supports targeted coaching and reevaluation.
takeaway: Revise teaching from observed learning difficulties.
learningObjective: Revise teaching from observed learning difficulties.

title: Health app appraisal
stem: A client wants an app to record migraine patterns for appointments. Which questions help judge whether it fits this purpose? Select all that apply.
options: Does it allow recording and exporting the relevant symptoms?
Is its clinical advice linked to credible identifiable sources?
Are favourable app-store ratings enough to establish accuracy?
How are sensitive health entries used or shared?
Is popularity a substitute for checking the intended function?
why: Relevant usable records support the client's stated appointment goal.
Identifiable evidence helps assess any accompanying advice.
Ratings reflect user experience, not necessarily clinical accuracy.
Privacy practices matter when storing sensitive information.
Popularity does not establish that the app meets this task.
takeaway: Evaluate a health app's purpose, evidence and privacy.
learningObjective: Evaluate a health app's purpose, evidence and privacy.

title: Setting an initial walking goal
stem: An inactive adult comfortably walks five minutes and wants to build a routine. Which initial plan best supports achievable progress over the next two weeks?
options: Resume the 30-minute daily route used several years ago
Agree on short scheduled walks and review tolerance after two weeks
Walk whenever motivation is high and record only the longest outing
Add distance every day to meet a preset target by day fourteen
why: A past capacity may exceed the current baseline.
The plan is specific, feasible and allows adjustment from actual response.
Irregular motivation-based activity may not build the desired routine.
Automatic increases may outpace tolerance and undermine persistence.
takeaway: Start activity goals from current capacity with planned review.
learningObjective: Start activity goals from current capacity with planned review.

title: Exploring ambivalence
stem: A client says, 'I know smoking harms me, but it helps me get through work.' What response best supports motivation?
options: List complications until the client agrees to quit
Set a quit date without discussion
Ask what the client likes and dislikes about smoking
Focus on whether coworkers approve of smoking
why: More warnings may not address the competing value the client describes.
An imposed goal may not reflect readiness.
Exploring both sides helps the client articulate reasons for change.
Coworker approval is less relevant than the client's goals and barriers.
takeaway: Explore ambivalence before prescribing a behaviour-change goal.
learningObjective: Explore ambivalence before prescribing a behaviour-change goal.

title: Learning from a smoking lapse
stem: After two weeks without smoking, a client smoked during an argument and feels the attempt is ruined. What should the nurse emphasize?
options: Review the trigger and adjust the quit plan
Restart the identical quit plan without discussing the argument
Count the lapse as proof of poor motivation
Focus exclusively on the number of cigarettes smoked
why: A lapse can identify coping supports needed for the next attempt.
Restarting the calendar alone may miss a coping gap revealed by the trigger.
One event does not establish lack of motivation.
Quantity alone does not explain the trigger or recovery plan.
takeaway: Use a lapse to refine cessation strategies rather than abandon the goal.
learningObjective: Use a lapse to refine cessation strategies rather than abandon the goal.

title: Changing sugary drink intake
stem: A client chooses replacing one daily soft drink with water as a first goal. What is the best nursing response?
options: Add several food changes to the goal at the same visit
Use daily weight as the main measure of the substitution
Provide general dietary education before specifying the routine
Confirm when the substitution will occur and how progress will be reviewed
why: Additional simultaneous goals may reduce feasibility before the chosen habit is established.
Weight change does not directly show whether the planned drink substitution occurred.
Information alone does not identify the cue and action needed for this chosen change.
A concrete cue and review plan strengthen implementation.
takeaway: Turn a chosen health behaviour into a practical routine and review plan.
learningObjective: Turn a chosen health behaviour into a practical routine and review plan.

title: Supporting tobacco cessation
stem: Which assessments help tailor a client's quit plan? Select all that apply.
options: Times and situations associated with smoking
Previous strategies that helped or failed
Whether the client meets the nurse's preferred quit date
Only the brand and purchase location
why: Trigger patterns identify where coping strategies are needed.
Past experience can reveal effective supports and barriers.
Goals should reflect collaborative planning rather than the nurse's preference.
Product details alone do not capture dependence or readiness.
takeaway: Tailor cessation support using triggers and prior attempts.
learningObjective: Tailor cessation support using triggers and prior attempts.

title: Adapting activity with knee pain
stem: A client with stable osteoarthritis develops knee pain during long walks but tolerates gentle cycling. They want better endurance. Which plan fits best?
options: Repeat the long walk daily until endurance improves
Agree on a lower-impact cycling trial with appropriate guidance
Use stretching alone as the endurance program
Pause activity until every episode of knee discomfort has ended
why: Repeating the painful load may reduce participation without addressing tolerability.
A tolerated lower-impact option can support the endurance goal.
Stretching alone does not provide equivalent endurance training.
Complete delay may worsen conditioning when a tolerable option exists.
takeaway: Match activity type to tolerated loading and the client's functional goal.
learningObjective: Match activity type to tolerated loading and the client's functional goal.

title: Activity after deconditioning
stem: After prolonged illness, a client walks only to the end of the corridor before tiring but wants to resume an old 40-minute route. What should the nurse recommend?
options: Resume the old route using the previous pace
Return on the date originally planned before the illness
Build gradually from current tolerance with the recovery team
Use flexibility exercises alone as the endurance plan
why: The old workload exceeds the stated current capacity.
Calendar timing does not establish regained function.
Graded progression reflects present ability and the endurance goal.
Flexibility may help movement but does not fully address endurance.
takeaway: Base post-illness activity progression on present function.
learningObjective: Base post-illness activity progression on present function.

title: Prolonged sitting at work
stem: A desk worker exercises on weekends but sits uninterrupted for several hours each workday. Which change most directly addresses the remaining pattern?
options: Schedule brief movement breaks during the workday
Add a longer exercise session on Saturday
Stand continuously at the same workstation all day
Record total weekly steps without altering work routines
why: Regular movement interrupts the prolonged sedentary periods identified.
Weekend exercise does not directly interrupt workday sitting.
Prolonged static standing is not the same as varied movement.
Tracking alone does not change uninterrupted sitting.
takeaway: Address long sedentary periods alongside planned exercise.
learningObjective: Address long sedentary periods alongside planned exercise.

title: Improving plant-food iron absorption
stem: A vegetarian client is improving dietary iron intake and often eats lentils at lunch. Which addition best supports absorption of the iron in that meal?
options: Tea served with the meal
A calcium supplement taken with the meal
Coffee immediately after the meal
Sweet peppers or another vitamin-C-rich food
why: Tea can reduce absorption of nonheme iron when taken with the meal.
Calcium taken with iron-rich meals may reduce iron absorption.
Coffee can inhibit nonheme iron absorption around the meal.
Vitamin C enhances absorption of iron from plant foods.
takeaway: Pair plant iron sources with vitamin-C-rich foods.
learningObjective: Pair plant iron sources with vitamin-C-rich foods.

title: Planning nutritious meals on a budget
stem: Which suggestions may help a client with limited income obtain balanced meals? Select all that apply.
options: Consider affordable frozen or canned foods with suitable labels
Plan meals using available low-cost protein foods
Recommend only fresh specialty produce
Assume all packaged foods have the same nutritional value
why: Appropriate frozen and canned options can be nutritious and affordable.
Feasible protein sources support nutrition within the budget.
Specialty-only advice may be financially inaccessible.
Labels and preparation vary, so blanket assumptions are inaccurate.
takeaway: Adapt nutrition teaching to cost and available food options.
learningObjective: Adapt nutrition teaching to cost and available food options.

title: Hydration in heat with restrictions
stem: An older adult with a prescribed fluid limit asks how to manage a heat wave. What is the best response?
options: Ignore the limit throughout the heat wave
Seek an individualized fluid and cooling plan from the treating team
Maintain the limit without considering new symptoms
Use sports drinks as unrestricted extra fluid
why: Unsupervised excess intake may worsen the condition requiring restriction.
The plan must balance heat risk with the client's clinical limitations.
Heat may change needs and symptoms requiring reassessment.
Sports drinks still contribute fluid and may add unwanted electrolytes.
takeaway: Individualize heat advice when medical fluid restrictions apply.
learningObjective: Individualize heat advice when medical fluid restrictions apply.

title: Protecting sleep during shift work
stem: A night-shift worker's daytime sleep is repeatedly interrupted by household noise and errands. Which plan best addresses the identified cause?
options: Extend sleep on days off while keeping workday arrangements
Wear an eye mask but remain available for daytime errands
Agree on a protected dark quiet sleep period with the household
Replace the main sleep period with brief naps in the living room
why: Catch-up sleep does not remove the recurring workday interruptions.
An eye mask does not address noise or expected availability.
Household agreement and an appropriate environment protect the actual sleep opportunity.
Fragmented naps in a busy setting may not provide adequate consolidated rest.
takeaway: Protect sleep opportunity and environment within shift-work constraints.
learningObjective: Protect sleep opportunity and environment within shift-work constraints.

title: Persistent snoring and sleepiness
stem: A client reports loud snoring, witnessed breathing pauses and daytime sleepiness despite enough time in bed. What should the nurse recommend?
options: Clinical assessment for a sleep-related breathing disorder
A larger pillow as the only intervention
More time in bed before mentioning breathing pauses
Caffeine at each meal to improve alertness
why: The combined symptoms warrant evaluation beyond sleep-hygiene advice.
Position changes alone do not evaluate reported breathing pauses.
Adequate sleep opportunity with apnea symptoms still needs assessment.
Stimulants may mask sleepiness without treating its cause.
takeaway: Refer breathing pauses with daytime sleepiness for assessment.
learningObjective: Refer breathing pauses with daytime sleepiness for assessment.

title: Clarifying social alcohol use
stem: A client describes drinking as social and asks about health effects. Which question should the nurse ask first to quantify the exposure?
options: What changes have you tried previously?
Do friends encourage you to drink?
What would you like to change?
What and how much do you drink in a usual week and on one occasion?
why: Previous attempts matter after the actual use pattern is clarified.
Social pressure adds context but does not quantify intake.
Goals help planning but do not establish current exposure.
Amount and pattern give meaning to the undefined label social.
takeaway: Quantify alcohol use before tailoring risk advice.
learningObjective: Quantify alcohol use before tailoring risk advice.

title: Preventive care with limited transportation
stem: Which approaches may improve preventive-care access for a rural client? Select all that apply.
options: Coordinate appropriate services during the same trip
Explore available transport assistance
Replace every examination with a phone call
Assume missed visits mean screening is unwanted
why: Coordinated visits can reduce travel burden when clinically feasible.
Practical transport support addresses an identified access barrier.
Some assessments require in-person examination or testing.
Access problems do not establish the client's preferences.
takeaway: Organize preventive care around real transportation constraints.
learningObjective: Organize preventive care around real transportation constraints.

title: Menopause symptom discussion
stem: A client experiencing bothersome hot flashes wants advice but is concerned about medication risks. What is the best initial approach?
options: Provide a general hot-flash booklet at the start of the visit
Assess symptom burden and individual treatment risks
Recommend hormones before reviewing contraindications
Focus only on laboratory confirmation before discussing coping
why: General information may help but does not establish this client's symptom burden or risks.
Severity, history and preferences guide a suitable treatment discussion.
Hormonal treatment requires individualized clinical review.
Practical support need not wait for routine laboratory confirmation.
takeaway: Individualize menopause counselling to symptom burden and clinical history.
learningObjective: Individualize menopause counselling to symptom burden and clinical history.

title: Postmenopausal bleeding
stem: A client who has had no periods for two years reports new vaginal spotting and asks if it can wait until a routine visit months away. What should the nurse advise?
options: Track it until it becomes heavy
Treat it as an expected menopause symptom
Arrange timely clinical assessment even if bleeding is light
Arrange routine cervical screening as the sole follow-up
why: Light bleeding still warrants evaluation after menopause.
New postmenopausal bleeding should not be presumed normal.
Assessment can identify the cause and appropriate follow-up.
Screening does not replace diagnostic assessment of new postmenopausal bleeding.
takeaway: Arrange assessment for new postmenopausal bleeding.
learningObjective: Arrange assessment for new postmenopausal bleeding.

title: Planning bone-health prevention
stem: A sedentary adult with a parent who sustained a hip fracture asks about preventing osteoporosis. Which plan best guides individualized prevention?
options: Arrange bone-risk review and tailor activity and nutrition
Start high-impact exercise based on prior fitness
Add calcium supplements as the entire prevention plan
Use flexibility exercise alone until bone-density testing
why: Family history and inactivity support individualized risk and prevention planning.
Past fitness does not establish suitability for high-impact loading now.
Calcium alone does not address activity, vitamin intake or overall fracture risk.
Flexibility alone does not address strength and appropriate weight-bearing goals.
takeaway: Tailor bone-health prevention to individual fracture risk and function.
learningObjective: Tailor bone-health prevention to individual fracture risk and function.

title: Height loss with new back discomfort
stem: An older adult reports new mid-back pain and a noticeable height reduction without a major fall. What should the nurse recommend?
options: Routine osteoporosis screening at the next annual visit
Treating presumed muscle strain before reviewing the height change
Starting posture exercises to correct the height loss
Prompt assessment for vertebral fracture or another cause
why: New pain and height change warrant earlier diagnostic assessment.
A presumed strain does not explain or evaluate the combined findings.
Exercise should not precede assessment of a possible fracture.
Vertebral fracture can occur without a major reported injury.
takeaway: Assess new back pain accompanied by height loss promptly.
learningObjective: Assess new back pain accompanied by height loss promptly.

title: Vision and healthy aging
stem: Which reported changes require evaluation rather than attribution to normal aging? Select all that apply.
options: New difficulty reading medication labels despite usual glasses
Gradual glare that limits night driving
Preference for brighter reading light without functional difficulty
Use of reading glasses prescribed at a recent examination
why: A new functional barrier may compromise medication safety.
Driving-limiting glare warrants assessment of vision and safety.
Lighting preference alone is less concerning without impairment.
Appropriate prescribed correction is not itself a warning finding.
takeaway: Evaluate visual changes that impair important daily activities.
learningObjective: Evaluate visual changes that impair important daily activities.

title: Hearing-related social withdrawal
stem: An older adult stops attending a discussion group because conversation is difficult in background noise. What is the best response?
options: Assume the client no longer enjoys social contact
Arrange hearing review and reduce background noise
Encourage lip-reading without discussing assessment
Provide written summaries of group discussions
why: Withdrawal may reflect a remediable communication barrier.
Assessment and a quieter setting address the barrier to the chosen discussion activity.
Lip-reading alone may not meet the client's needs.
Summaries convey information but do not restore the desired conversational participation.
takeaway: Address hearing barriers that reduce social participation.
learningObjective: Address hearing barriers that reduce social participation.

title: Urinary urgency and community activity
stem: An older adult avoids outings because of urinary urgency but has not discussed it with a clinician. What should the nurse do?
options: Recommend accepting it as unavoidable aging
Suggest avoiding fluids before every outing
Encourage assessment and individualized continence strategies
Use absorbent pads for outings as the ongoing plan
why: Urgency may have treatable contributors and warrants assessment.
Broad restriction can create dehydration without resolving the cause.
Evaluation can support continence and valued activities.
Containment can help temporarily but does not establish the cause or tailored treatment.
takeaway: Promote assessment of continence concerns that limit daily life.
learningObjective: Promote assessment of continence concerns that limit daily life.

title: Nutrition after a partner's death
stem: An older adult has lost weight since the partner who shopped and cooked died. Oral examination and swallowing are reassuring; the client often skips meals because food is unavailable. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: Assess shopping and meal access and arrange suitable practical support
Request a new swallowing assessment before discussing meals
Offer a lower-fat menu as the first intervention
Ask the client to count calories before arranging food access
why: The findings point to a practical food-access gap requiring support.
Current evidence does not identify swallowing as the principal barrier.
Restriction does not address skipped meals and weight loss.
Tracking does not make needed food available.
takeaway: Match nutrition support to the identified practical cause of reduced intake.
learningObjective: Match nutrition support to the identified practical cause of reduced intake.

title: Driving and functional change
stem: An older adult reports recent near misses and difficulty judging distances when driving. What should the nurse recommend?
options: Continue driving because no collision has occurred
Rely on age alone to decide fitness
Restrict driving only when family members insist
Arrange prompt assessment and discuss interim transport and safety plans
why: Near misses may indicate meaningful risk before a collision occurs.
Functional ability, not age alone, guides assessment.
Family concern is useful but not required to act on symptoms.
Assessment and practical alternatives address safety and independence together.
takeaway: Respond to driving-related functional changes with assessment and transport planning.
learningObjective: Respond to driving-related functional changes with assessment and transport planning.

title: Maintaining independence at home
stem: Which assessments help tailor health-promotion support for an older adult living alone? Select all that apply.
options: Ability to obtain and prepare food
Ability to manage appointments and medications
Chronological age as the sole measure of support need
Family preference without asking the client
why: Food access and preparation affect nutrition and independence.
Complex daily tasks reveal practical support needs.
Age alone does not establish functional ability.
The client's goals and choices remain central to planning.
takeaway: Assess everyday function rather than assuming needs from age.
learningObjective: Assess everyday function rather than assuming needs from age.

title: Social connection after retirement
stem: A recently retired client feels isolated and wants more contact but dislikes large groups. Which suggestion best fits the goal?
options: Enrol in the largest available senior club
Explore a small regular activity linked to an existing interest
Offer a general list of social services to review independently
Arrange several unfamiliar activities without asking preferences
why: Group size may reproduce the barrier the client describes.
A preferred manageable activity supports feasible sustained connection.
A broad list may not connect the client's interests with a manageable recurring activity.
Imposed unfamiliar activities may not support engagement.
takeaway: Match social-connection opportunities to the client's interests and comfort.
learningObjective: Match social-connection opportunities to the client's interests and comfort.

title: Discussing sexuality in later life
stem: An older adult asks about sexual activity after beginning a new relationship. What approach best supports health promotion?
options: Discuss only urinary symptoms
Assume infection prevention is unnecessary after menopause
Offer private, respectful assessment of sexual goals and prevention needs
Ask the adult's children to identify appropriate advice
why: Urinary symptoms do not cover sexual-health needs.
Infection exposure remains possible regardless of fertility.
Individual assessment avoids assumptions and supports relevant counselling.
The capable adult's privacy and preferences guide the discussion.
takeaway: Include sexual health in older-adult assessment without age-based assumptions.
learningObjective: Include sexual health in older-adult assessment without age-based assumptions.

title: Advance-care conversations
stem: A healthy older adult asks when to tell family what matters if serious illness occurs. What should the nurse suggest?
options: Begin values-based discussions while the client can participate fully
Wait until an emergency determines the available choices
Ask family to select preferences independently
Focus only on completing a form without discussion
why: Early discussion helps others understand values before a crisis.
Emergencies may reduce time and ability for considered conversation.
The client's values should guide planning.
Forms alone may not communicate the meaning behind choices.
takeaway: Encourage early discussion of values for future health decisions.
learningObjective: Encourage early discussion of values for future health decisions.

title: Caregiver health maintenance
stem: A caregiver misses their own appointments because the care recipient cannot stay alone. What is the best nursing response?
options: Remind them more firmly that appointments matter
Repeatedly reschedule appointments around the existing care routine
Provide another screening brochure only
Explore respite or replacement support for appointment times
why: The caregiver already identifies a practical rather than informational barrier.
The supervision gap may persist unless replacement care becomes available.
A brochure does not provide supervision for the care recipient.
Targeted replacement support can enable the caregiver's own preventive care.
takeaway: Address caregiving barriers to the caregiver's health maintenance.
learningObjective: Address caregiving barriers to the caregiver's health maintenance.

title: Evaluating a community walking program
stem: Which outcomes best indicate that a new accessible walking group is meeting its health-promotion goal? Select all that apply.
options: Participants attend regularly and report manageable exertion
Participants sustain agreed activity goals over time
The program printed many flyers
Staff delivered every planned education session
why: Participation with tolerable effort supports feasibility of the program.
Sustained behaviour is more informative than one-time interest.
Distribution volume measures promotion activity rather than participant outcomes.
Session delivery measures implementation rather than participants' sustained activity outcomes.
takeaway: Evaluate health-promotion programs using meaningful participation and behaviour outcomes.
learningObjective: Evaluate health-promotion programs using meaningful participation and behaviour outcomes.
